newsitem.title: FRANCE: Jospin wants fairer farm subsidies.
newsitem.headline: Jospin wants fairer farm subsidies.

text.p: New Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin pledged on Thursday to look for fairer ways of distributing subsidies to farmers.

In a keynote speech to parliament, Jospin kept alive hopes of major legislation to define rural priorities for a generation -- a so-called orientation law first drafted by the previous centre-right government and strongly defended by farm groups.
He also pledged to give priority to helping young agricultural workers into their first jobs.
But he appeared to challenge some of France's "grain baron" farmers, who see their subsidies under threat, by suggesting their European Union payments should be spread out more thinly.
"We will seek variations in support and greater fairness in the way they are delivered," he said.

France is a major beneficiary of EU subsidies under the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), helping its farmers to export enough cereals and other goods to make up roughly half the country's 100 billion franc annual trade surplus.

But the Socialist party, swept to office at the head of a broad-left coalition three weeks ago, has long said it favours fairer distribution of the EU aid, which is weighted heavily towards a minority.
About 80 percent of cash allocated to French cereals from the $50 billion EU farm budget goes to 20 percent of the farmers actually involved, the French wheat producers' association says.
Beef and dairy producers also get significant EU aid.
But others, notably fruit and vegetable producers, get nothing from the CAP, and have waged a noisy campaign for protection from cheap foreign imports in the past year.
Scenting the new government's mood for change, the AGPB wheat association tried to sell the idea of gradual reforms at its annual meeting in Dijon, eastern France, on Wednesday.
But several of its senior members told the meeting they would refuse to consider any reduction in compensation.

Socialist Farm Minister Louis Le Pensec told the same gathering the public wanted its money spent fairly. But he said he opposed one idea from the EU's Brussels-based Commission that cereals aid should be cut across the board in order to pay for the cost of last year's European beef crisis.

The Commission says its farm subsidies will have to be substantially altered to allow for the EU's planned eastward expansion after the turn of the century. But the EU is divided over how deep the reforms should go.

The current system offers both compensation for cuts in support prices agreed in the major overhaul of the CAP in 1992 and export subsidies to help farmers compete abroad. Indirect support comes from import tariff barriers.
In one of the most controversial policies, which France wants phased out, the CAP also pays farmers to keep some farm land idle in set-aside schemes to balance supply and demand.
